query: In high-entropy alloys, what governs superconducting behavior and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, identify a controlled comparison against a baseline that could reveal the governing cause, predict the relative observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, define its boundary conditions, state what prior evidence would make it plausible, and specify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In single-phase, body-centered-cubic (bcc) high-entropy alloys, the superconducting transition temperature (Tc) is maximized when the alloy’s average valence-electron concentration (VEC, expressed as electrons per atom) is tuned to ≈ 6.75 ± 0.15 because this VEC optimizes the density of states at the Fermi level and strengthens electron–phonon coupling in the bcc lattice.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic or near-equiatomic bcc high-entropy alloy composed of 5–7 transition-metal elements (e.g., Nb–Ti–Zr–Hf–Ta system) processed to the same grain size, residual resistivity ratio, and impurity content.
generation.intervention: Systematic compositional adjustment that varies the average VEC from 6.0 to 7.4 in 0.1-step increments by partially substituting constituent elements while preserving the single-phase bcc structure.
generation.conditions: Measurements at ambient pressure, zero magnetic field, with temperature swept from 10 K down to 0.3 K in a dilution refrigerator.
generation.structural_mediator: The un‐distorted bcc lattice with a narrow distribution of nearest-neighbor bond lengths (<2 %).
generation.mechanism: Tuning the VEC modifies band filling near the Fermi level; at VEC ≈ 6.75, a van Hove–like peak in the electronic density of states aligns with EF, raising N(EF). Larger N(EF) increases the electron–phonon coupling constant λ according to McMillan theory, thereby raising Tc.
generation.predicted_outcome: A dome-shaped Tc(VEC) curve peaking at VEC ≈ 6.75 with Tc about twice that of alloys at VEC ≈ 6.0 or 7.4. The electron–phonon coupling constant extracted from specific-heat and tunnelling data will exhibit the same maximum near 6.75.
generation.baseline: An otherwise identical bcc HEA whose VEC is fixed at 6.0 (e.g., Nb25Ti25Zr25Hf25) is expected to show the lower-Tc side of the dome, with Tc at least 50 % lower than the optimized composition.
generation.boundary: Applies only to single-phase bcc HEAs with low impurity scattering (mean free path >5 nm) and without magnetic elements (no 3d Fe, Co, Ni); deviations expected if (i) a second phase precipitates, (ii) the lattice becomes fcc or hcp, (iii) magnetic impurities exceed 0.1 at %, or (iv) external pressure alters the band structure.
generation.uncertainty: The exact VEC value at which the density-of-states peak occurs may vary ±0.1 depending on alloy-specific band structure; local lattice distortions in highly size-mismatched HEAs could broaden the peak and flatten the Tc dome.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a compositional series of five-element bcc HEAs whose average VEC is 6.0, 6.4, 6.6, 6.75, 7.0, and 7.4 while maintaining identical processing. Measure Tc via four-probe resistivity and specific heat. Determine λ and N(EF) from low-temperature specific heat and electron tunnelling spectroscopy.
measurements: Superconducting transition temperature Tc from resistivity and heat-capacity onset
Low-temperature electronic specific-heat coefficient γ (proportional to N(EF))
Electron–phonon coupling constant λ via McMillan–Dynes fit to tunnelling spectra
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If Tc, γ, and λ do not show a maximum (within experimental error) near VEC ≈ 6.75 but instead increase monotonically, remain flat, or peak elsewhere (>0.2 VEC units away), the hypothesis is falsified.
